name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MATCH_Q01 - Animal breeding methods and examples

questiontext.text:
Match the animal breeding methods with their corresponding descriptions or examples:

List I (Breeding Method)List II (Description / Example)
(A) Inbreeding(i) Mule
(B) Out-crossing(ii) Mating of closely related individuals within the same breed for 4–6 generations
(C) Cross-breeding(iii) Hisardale sheep developed from Bikaneri ewes and Marino rams
(D) Interspecific hybridisation(iv) Mating within the same breed with no common ancestors for 4–6 generations

Choose the correct option:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Animal breeding strategies are broadly divided into inbreeding (mating within the same breed among closely related individuals) and out-breeding (mating of unrelated animals).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Inbreeding refers to the mating of more closely related individuals within the same breed for 4 to 6 generations to increase homozygosity.
2. Out-crossing is the mating of animals within the same breed that have no common ancestors on either side of their pedigree up to 4 to 6 generations.
3. Cross-breeding involves mating superior males of one breed with superior females of another breed, as exemplified by Hisardale, a sheep breed developed in Punjab by crossing Bikaneri ewes and Marino rams.
4. Interspecific hybridisation involves mating male and female animals of two different related species, such as in the production of the mule.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Inbreeding with mating of closely related individuals within the same breed for 4–6 generations; Out-crossing with mating within the same breed with no common ancestors for 4–6 generations; Cross-breeding with Hisardale sheep; and Interspecific hybridisation with mule.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MATCH_Q02 - Disease-resistant crop varieties and target pathogens

questiontext.text:
Match the improved crop varieties with the diseases to which they are resistant:

List I (Crop Variety)List II (Resistance to Disease)
(A) Himgiri (Wheat)(i) Bacterial blight
(B) Pusa swarnim (Brassica)(ii) Chilli mosaic virus, Tobacco mosaic virus and Leaf curl
(C) Pusa Komal (Cowpea)(iii) Leaf and stripe rust, hill bunt
(D) Pusa Sadabahar (Chilli)(iv) White rust

Choose the correct option:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Conventional plant breeding by hybridisation and selection has produced several crop cultivars resistant to fungal, bacterial, and viral pathogens.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Himgiri is a wheat variety resistant to leaf and stripe rust as well as hill bunt.
2. Pusa swarnim (Karan rai) is a Brassica variety resistant to white rust.
3. Pusa Komal is a cowpea variety resistant to bacterial blight.
4. Pusa Sadabahar is a chilli variety resistant to chilli mosaic virus, tobacco mosaic virus, and leaf curl.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings match Himgiri with leaf and stripe rust and hill bunt, Pusa swarnim with white rust, Pusa Komal with bacterial blight, and Pusa Sadabahar with chilli mosaic virus, tobacco mosaic virus, and leaf curl.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MATCH_Q03 - Insect pest-resistant crops and target pests

questiontext.text:
Match the crop varieties or traits with the insect pests against which they confer resistance:

List I (Crop / Trait)List II (Insect Pest)
(A) Brassica – Pusa Gaurav(i) Shoot and fruit borer
(B) Flat bean – Pusa Sem 2(ii) Stem sawfly
(C) Okra (Bhindi) – Pusa Sawani(iii) Aphids
(D) Wheat – Solid stems(iv) Jassids, aphids and fruit borer

Choose the correct option:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Host plant resistance to insect pests may result from morphological traits (such as solid stems or hairy leaves) or from specific varieties bred through hybridisation and selection.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Pusa Gaurav is a variety of Brassica (rapeseed mustard) resistant to aphids.
2. Pusa Sem 2 (along with Pusa Sem 3) is a flat bean variety resistant to jassids, aphids, and fruit borer.
3. Pusa Sawani (along with Pusa A-4) is an okra (bhindi) variety resistant to shoot and fruit borer.
4. Solid stems in wheat lead to non-preference by the stem sawfly.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings match Pusa Gaurav with aphids, Pusa Sem 2 with jassids, aphids and fruit borer, Pusa Sawani with shoot and fruit borer, and solid stems in wheat with stem sawfly.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MATCH_Q04 - Biofortified crops and enhanced nutritional traits

questiontext.text:
Match the biofortified crops or varieties with their specific nutritional improvements:

List I (Biofortified Crop / Variety)List II (Nutritional Improvement)
(A) Wheat (Atlas 66)(i) Over five times as much iron as commonly consumed varieties
(B) Maize hybrids (developed in 2000)(ii) Enriched with vitamin C
(C) Iron-fortified rice(iii) High protein content
(D) Bitter gourd and bathua (IARI)(iv) Twice the amount of lysine and tryptophan

Choose the correct option:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biofortification involves breeding crops with higher levels of vitamins, minerals, protein, or healthier fats to combat hidden hunger and improve public health.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Atlas 66 is a wheat variety with high protein content that has been used as a donor for improving cultivated wheat.
2. Maize hybrids developed in 2000 contain twice the amount of the amino acids lysine and tryptophan compared to existing maize hybrids.
3. Iron-fortified rice contains over five times as much iron as commonly consumed rice varieties.
4. The Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI), New Delhi, released vitamin C-enriched bitter gourd, bathua, mustard, and tomato.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings match Atlas 66 with high protein content, maize hybrids (2000) with twice the amount of lysine and tryptophan, iron-fortified rice with over five times as much iron, and bitter gourd and bathua with vitamin C enrichment.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MATCH_Q05 - Tissue culture and single cell protein concepts

questiontext.text:
Match the terms and organisms in tissue culture and single cell protein production with their correct descriptions:

List I (Term / Organism)List II (Description)
(A) Totipotency(i) Genetically identical plants produced through micro-propagation
(B) Somaclones(ii) Capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant
(C) Spirulina(iii) Bacterium capable of producing 25 tonnes of protein due to high growth rate
(D) Methylophilus methylotrophus(iv) Blue-green alga grown on starch-rich waste water as protein-rich food

Choose the correct option:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Tissue culture relies on cellular totipotency to regenerate plants in vitro, whereas Single Cell Protein (SCP) uses fast-growing microbes as an alternative protein source.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Totipotency is the capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant under sterile conditions in a nutrient medium.
2. Somaclones are plants produced by micro-propagation that are genetically identical to the original plant from which they were grown.
3. Spirulina is a blue-green alga that can be grown easily on waste water from potato processing plants (containing starch), straw, molasses, and sewage to serve as protein-rich food.
4. Methylophilus methylotrophus is a bacterial species expected to produce 25 tonnes of protein because of its high rate of biomass production and growth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings match totipotency with the capacity to regenerate a whole plant from an explant, somaclones with genetically identical micro-propagated plants, Spirulina with the blue-green alga grown on starch-rich waste water, and Methylophilus methylotrophus with the bacterium producing 25 tonnes of protein.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MATCH_Q06 - Chronological sequence of steps in plant breeding

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following main steps involved in breeding a new genetic variety of a crop in the correct chronological sequence:

  • P. Selection and testing of superior recombinants
  • Q. Evaluation and selection of parents
  • R. Collection of variability (germplasm collection)
  • S. Testing, release and commercialisation of new cultivars
  • T. Cross hybridisation among the selected parents

Choose the correct sequence:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Systematic plant breeding programmes follow five sequential stages to develop, stabilise, and release a new crop cultivar.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Sequencing
1. First, genetic variability is collected and preserved from wild varieties and relatives, forming the germplasm collection.
2. Second, the germplasm is evaluated to select parents with desirable combinations of characters, which are multiplied and purelines created where possible.
3. Third, the selected parents are cross-hybridised to combine desired traits from two different plants into hybrids.
4. Fourth, superior recombinants among the hybrid progeny are selected, scientifically evaluated, and self-pollinated for several generations until homozygosity is achieved.
5. Fifth, the newly selected lines are tested in research fields and farmers' fields for at least three growing seasons across agroclimatic zones before release and commercialisation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is: Collection of variability → Evaluation and selection of parents → Cross hybridisation among the selected parents → Selection and testing of superior recombinants → Testing, release and commercialisation of new cultivars.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER9_MATCH_Q07 - Crop varieties, pathogens, and pest resistance traits

questiontext.text:
Match the crop varieties, plant diseases, and resistance traits with their correct descriptions:

List I (Item)List II (Description)
(A) Jaya and Ratna(i) Fungal disease of crops
(B) Parbhani kranti(ii) Semi-dwarf rice varieties developed in India
(C) Smooth-leaved, nectar-less cotton(iii) Yellow mosaic virus-resistant bhindi developed by gene transfer from a wild species
(D) Red rot of sugarcane(iv) Morphological trait that does not attract bollworms

Choose the correct option:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Crop improvement in India has combined semi-dwarf high-yielding varieties, wild-relative gene transfer for disease resistance, and morphological traits for insect pest resistance.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Jaya and Ratna are better-yielding semi-dwarf rice varieties developed in India.
2. Parbhani kranti is a variety of bhindi (Abelmoschus esculentus) in which resistance to yellow mosaic virus was transferred from a wild species.
3. Smooth-leaved and nectar-less cotton varieties do not attract bollworms.
4. Red rot of sugarcane, along with brown rust of wheat and late blight of potato, is a disease caused by fungi.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings match Jaya and Ratna with semi-dwarf rice varieties developed in India, Parbhani kranti with yellow mosaic virus-resistant bhindi, smooth-leaved and nectar-less cotton with non-attraction to bollworms, and red rot of sugarcane with a fungal disease.
